section_summary: This section concludes a photographic record of the catastrophic July 1938 Kobe floods, followed by Japan Chronicle reports on the disaster and the disputed claim that subway passengers had died. Consular despatches then document further August flooding in Kobe and Taiwan, the resulting transportation and agricultural damage, Kobe’s relief and reconstruction needs, and proposed flood-control engineering. The final pages concern flood-relief accounts and cross-references to later typhoon damage in the Kantō and Shikoku regions and to a proposed American donation to Kobe.

subfiles.title: Photograph captions documenting the Kobe flood, views 7–67
subfiles.about: Captions identify flood destruction throughout Kobe and rank the extent of damage in the city’s eight wards.
subfiles.summary: The photographs show buried and destroyed houses, newly cut streambeds, damaged bridges and railway facilities, heavy silt deposits, and devastation around the Uji, Ōishi, and Sumiyoshi rivers. Numerous views document Kitanochō, Nada, Minato, Sannomiya, Motomachi, Nunobiki, and other parts of Kobe, including the damaged consulate and the home of Consul Walter P. McConaughy. The final page ranks Nada as the most severely affected ward, followed by Fukiai, Soto, Minato, Kobe, Suma, Hayashida, and Hyogo.

subfiles.title: Hanshin Denies Subway Rumours
subfiles.about: The Hanshin Tram Company and police deny rumors that passengers died in the flooded subway.
subfiles.summary: Hanshin expected to restore subway service between Sannomiya and Iwaya after removing the remaining mud near the Onohama Line viaduct. Management stated that all passengers escaped safely and that their belongings were returned. Superintendent Tomihisa credited Sergeants Kitamura and Matsumura with directing evacuations from cars at Motomachi, Sannomiya, and Kasugano.

subfiles.title: Kobe Swept by Floods
subfiles.about: A pictorial report describes the July 5 Kobe flood’s casualties, destruction, and geographic extent.
subfiles.summary: The supplement calls the flood the worst disaster in Kobe’s history, estimating more than 800 deaths, roughly ¥100 million in property loss, and widespread destruction of homes, bridges, roads, farmland, and forests. It describes torrents and landslides sweeping through Aotani, Kanochō, Minatogawa, Ōishigawa, Sumiyoshi, and other districts, while noting damage extending toward Nishinomiya, Takarazuka, Arima, Sanda, and Shioya. Statistical tables summarize casualties and material losses, and accompanying photographs show the Daimaru and Sogo stores, Kanochō, Aotani Creek, Tor Hotel, Ikuta-mae, and the obstructed Hanshin highway.

subfiles.title: Hanshin Denies Subway Rumours
subfiles.about: A duplicate clipping reports that Hanshin subway passengers escaped the flood safely.
subfiles.summary: Hanshin reported that mud removal was nearly complete and anticipated reopening service east of Sannomiya. The company rejected reports of passenger deaths. Superintendent Tomihisa stated that Sergeants Kitamura and Matsumura ensured the evacuation of trains at Motomachi, Sannomiya, and Kasugano.

subfiles.title: Property Damage by Heavy Rains in Taiwan
subfiles.about: The despatch reports railway, flood-control, housing, and agricultural damage caused by typhoon rains in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Heavy rains after a long dry period damaged railways at more than 100 points in Hsinchu Prefecture, washing out bridges and track foundations and causing flooding, silting, and tunnel collapses. Material shortages prevented early restoration of the coast line, while efforts focused on the newer mountain route through Zhunan to Taichung. Dikes on the lower Tamsui River were endangered, and Hsinchu reported missing persons, destroyed or flooded houses, and damaged rice fields, although the foreign community had suffered only inconvenience.

subfiles.title: Flood Situation at Kobe, Japan
subfiles.from: L. H. Gourley, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: The despatch assesses renewed flooding, relief work, financing, and long-term engineering problems after the July 5 Kobe disaster.
subfiles.summary: Downpours on August 1–2 and August 19 caused renewed flooding, railway and tram interruptions, landslides, additional crop damage, and partial reversal of earlier clearance work. Gourley reports vigorous local relief efforts but argues that the central government’s proposed subsidy was inadequate compared with the estimated ¥350 million in damage and Kobe’s contemplated ¥200 million reconstruction bond. Proposed preventive works included reforestation, wider and deeper river channels, stronger and higher bridges, a northern flood rampart, a second Kobe–Osaka highway, expanded storm sewers, and restoration of silted reservoirs. The despatch also discusses water rationing, epidemic risk, silt disposal, damage in Ehime, and the floods’ fiscal and economic effects.

subfiles.title: Damage by Heavy Rains in Taiwan
subfiles.about: The despatch supplies additional estimates of agricultural, railway, urban, and road damage from Taiwan’s August rains.
subfiles.summary: Damage in Hsinchu Prefecture was estimated at ¥8.44 million, including thousands of acres of rice fields and other farmland and large quantities of drying rice. Railway chief Keinoshin Watanabe estimated railway losses at ¥1.5 million and said delayed preventive repairs had worsened the destruction. Flooding also affected Dajia, Tainan, and Kaohsiung, while a landslide closed the east-coast road between Su’ao and Hualien.

subfiles.title: Accounts and Returns—Special Account Under Authorization No. 29
subfiles.from: L. H. Gourley, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Gourley transmits the August accounts for an American donation to Kobe flood relief.
subfiles.summary: The letter forwards the consulate’s special accounts and returns for August 1–31, 1938. The enclosed forms document a disbursement made as a donation to the City of Kobe for flood relief.

subfiles.title: Document File Note for Report No. 3308
subfiles.about: The file note cross-references a report on a record Kantō typhoon and a later gale over Shikoku.
subfiles.summary: The note points to Report No. 3308 concerning the record typhoon that struck the Kantō area on September 1 and the strong gale that struck Shikoku on September 5. It files the report by reference under the calamities subject.

subfiles.title: X. Miscellaneous: September Typhoon Damage and Air-Raid Maneuvers
subfiles.about: The report summarizes September storm losses in Kantō and Shikoku and notes regional air-raid exercises.
subfiles.summary: A record typhoon on September 1 reportedly killed at least fifty people, flooded or destroyed thousands of homes, damaged shipping around Yokohama, and disrupted communications. A September 5 gale caused further damage in Shikoku, and the combined typhoon losses affected more than one million acres of cultivated land. The page also records extensive Kantō anti-air-raid maneuvers held September 12–16.

subfiles.title: Document File Note on Proposed Donation to Kobe
subfiles.about: The note cross-references McConaughy’s proposal for a small federal donation to Kobe flood relief.
subfiles.summary: McConaughy suggested that the United States Government give $100–$150 to Kobe municipality as appreciation for the expedited clearance of streets leading to the American Consulate after the July 5 flood. The proposed sum was to be used for municipal flood-relief work.
